title: Teacher development for retention: grow the conditions, not just the teacher
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Hughes proposes a 'Teacher Development Garden' metaphor as an alternative to the ladder model of CPD, arguing teachers do not grow simply because someone tells them to but because the conditions around them make growth possible. She maps eight elements onto the metaphor - soil (belonging and fit), roots (relationships), trunk (agency and professional identity), branches (expertise pathways), sunlight (purpose and meaning), water (resources and conditions), the greenhouse (sustainable school design) and pruning (feedback and coaching) - with 'weather' (workload, low trust, initiative overload) as the external threat. Her sharpest structural critique is that schools often improve only one part of the garden at a time - more CPD but no time, more coaching but no agency - leaving retention efforts scattered and shallow. The piece closes by reframing retention not as a wellbeing poster but as 'the design of the working environment'.
points: Hughes's 'Teacher Development Garden' metaphor reframes CPD from a linear ladder every teacher climbs identically to an ecosystem requiring multiple simultaneous conditions to sustain growth.

Her critique that schools typically fix only one element at a time - 'more CPD, but no time... more coaching, but no agency' - names a common but underexamined pattern of well-intentioned but ineffective retention strategy.
She reframes retention explicitly as system design rather than morale management: 'Retention is not a wellbeing poster. It is the design of the working environment.'

Her inclusion of 'weather' (workload, low trust, initiative overload) as an external factor outside the garden itself distinguishes conditions leaders control from conditions imposed on them by wider system pressures.
quotes: Teachers stay when they are rooted in a school: connected to colleagues, trusted by leaders, able to grow, resourced to do the job well, and able to imagine a future there. Development is not separate from retention. It is one of the main ways schools create reasons to stay.
The soil is belonging and fit. This is the foundation. Without good soil, development does not take root.
The greenhouse is sustainable school design. Retention is not a wellbeing poster. It is the design of the working environment.
Schools often try to retain teachers by focusing on only one part of the garden. They offer more CPD, but no time. More coaching, but no agency. More wellbeing, but no workload change.

The old model says: train the teacher, send them back to the classroom, hope they stay. A better model says: build the soil, strengthen the roots, grow the trunk, protect the greenhouse, water the work, prune with care, and watch for the weather.
